ex-501-1.title: Range of α radiation in air
ex-501-1.question:
The figure shows the set-up used to determine the range of α radiation in air.

Before the α source is introduced, the counter shows a count rate of around 20 min–1. Then, the α source is brought near the GM tube. The distance d between them

is measured by a ruler. As the source is moved away from the GM tube, the corresponding count rate R is recorded. The following table shows the result.

(a) Why does the GM counter record a non-zero count rate even when there is no α source in front of it?

(b) What is the count rate solely due to the α source when d = 2 cm?

(c) Estimate the range of this α source. Explain briefly.
ex-501-1.answer:
(a) The non-zero count rate is due to background radiation.

(b) Count rate due to α source = 68 – 20 = 48 min–1

(c) The range of the source is about 3.5 cm.

When the source is 3.5 cm away from the GM tube, R drops to about the same as the background count rate.

ex-501-2.title: Distinguish radiation using different absorbers
ex-501-2.question:
A small fragment of radioactive ore is put in a lead box with a small opening. A GM tube connected to a counter is put in front of the opening.

Different absorbers are put between the ore fragment and the GM tube in turn and the corresponding count rates are recorded below.

Absorber

Count rate / min–1

—

302

A sheet of paper

298

5-mm aluminium plate

33

25-mm lead block

29

50-mm lead block

32

(a) Explain whether the ore emits

(i) α radiation;

(ii) β radiation;

(iii) γ radiation.

(b) Estimate the background count rate. Explain briefly.
ex-501-2.answer:
(a) (i) A piece of paper can stop α radiation. Since the count rate does not drop significantly when the paper is used as the absorber, the ore does not emit α radiation.

(ii) A 5-mm aluminium plate can stop β radiation. Since the count rate shows a significant drop when the aluminium block is used as the absorber, the ore emits β radiation.

(iii) Lead blocks can absorb some γ radiation. Since the count rate does not show further significant drop when lead blocks of different thicknesses replace the aluminium block, the ore does not emit γ radiation.

(b) A lead block can absorb all β radiation. When a 50-mm lead block is used, the remaining count rate is due to the background radiation. The background count rate is around 30 counts per minute. Exercise 1.2 Q10 (p.26)
ex-501-2.tips:
Skill

Problem-solving

Radiations and absorbers ① Identify the type of radiation that can be absorbed by each absorber. ② Start from the weakest absorber. ③ Compare the count rates. Since an absorber may be able to absorb more than one type of radiation, you need to compare the counts rates between cases of different absorbers, not just with the case with no absorber.

ex-501-3.title: Film badge
ex-501-3.question:
Radiation workers need to wear film badges to monitor their exposure to radiation during work (Fig a). The film badge consists of a 5-mm aluminium slab, a 5-mm lead slab and a photographic film in a plastic wrapping (Fig b). The film is developed in regular time intervals. The degree of blackening of different areas of the film shows the level of exposure to β and γ radiation.

In each of the following cases, compare and explain the degree of blackening of different areas of the film after it has been developed.

(a) The worker is exposed to β radiation only.

(b) The worker is exposed to γ radiation only.
ex-501-3.answer:
(a) Area X is blackened because the plastic wrapping cannot block β radiation effectively. Areas Y and Z are not blackened because β radiation is completely blocked by the aluminium slab and lead slab.

(b) Areas X and Y show similar degree of blackening because the plastic wrapping and the aluminium slab cannot block γ radiation effectively. Area Z is the least blackened because the lead slab can partly block γ radiation. This area receives the least amount of radiation.
